newsitem.title: INDIA: India rail network's safety record improves slowly.
newsitem.headline: India rail network's safety record improves slowly.

text.p: Better equipment has helped India's accident-prone railway network to improve its safety record, but mishaps at railway crossings and sabotage continue to be major problems, officials said on Thursday.
"There has been a reduction in the number of accidents," an official of the goverment's Railway Board, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.

India's railways cover a vast network spread over 62,915 km (39,321 miles) and in 1995/96 carried 123 million passengers on long-distance journeys involving more than 500 km. Trains are the cheapest mode of travel in the sprawling country.
The railway official said that accidents have been caused by wagon faults, track defects and human error, but the railways had used new techniques to strengthen the network and step up checks.
The government said in a report this week that 594 people died in 398 accidents in 1995/96 (April-March), compared with 305 deaths in 501 accidents the previous year.

The official said the government measured safety on railway networks by the number of accidents per million kilometres (620,000 miles) of train journeys. This had come down to 0.61 per million train km in 1995/96 from two in 1975/76.
In the current year, there have been 306 accidents until the end of January, compared with 313 in the same period of 1995/96, the official said.
The record is improving slowly, but accidents continue to occur regularly. In the past decade there have been more than 30 serious rail accidents.

In August 1995, around 350 people were killed in India's worst train accident in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh near the town of Ferozabad, 200 km (125 miles) from New Delhi, when two trains collided in an accident blamed on human error.
At least 33 people died in a bomb attack on a train in the northeastern state of Assam in December.
"Sabotage has been the cause of many serious accidents," Railway Minister Ram Vilas Paswan said in parliament on Wednesday, when he presented the railway budget for 1997/98.
He was referring to attacks or damage to rail tracks caused by separatist or militant groups.
Paswan said there more than 24,500 railway crossings which were still unmanned. "An...area of concern has been level crossing accidents due to rash and careless driving of road vehicles," he said.

The official said the railways had begun a process of strengthening tracks by using heavier 60 kg (132 lb) rails as against the 40 kg (90 lb) rails used earlier. Old-fashioned fish plates are being replaced by welded rails.

"For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics of the track, sophisticated track recording cars, oscillograph cars and portable accelrators are being progressively used," the government report said.
The report added that ultrasonic equipment was being used to detect axle problems in railway carriages. As many as 296 of the 398 train accidents in 1995/96 occurred when trains ran off the tracks.
Old wagons were also being gradually replaced, the official said. "Like any overaged stock, they must be phased out."
